It only takes processing power if you intend to control the volume while it is still a digital signal. If you do this in the analog section of the audio, say right before the power amplifier, then you only need a handful of simple electronic components to make an automatic gain control (AGC) circuit or a limiter/compressor to fit the audio into a given volume envelope. We've become to reliant on solving every problem with software and processors that we ignore the simplicity that can be had from using traditional analog electronics to accomplish the same thing. Many older TVs had these kinds of features but people did not know they were there and didn't use them so the manufacturers started leaving them out to save money.

Its a lot easier for manufacturers to do things in software because software is essentially free where as hardware costs, even if it costs just a few cent its a few cents that manufacturers just don't want to spend.

But in the case of most consumer media devices including TVs the audio and/or video data is not necessarily available to the main processor. Most of the hardware involves some dedicated purpose built chips that handle the decoding and processing so they simply cannot be re-programmed to do a new function. This is because it is cheaper to use application specific chips that can be bought cheaply in large quantities than to essentially turn a multi-function computer into a TV. Hardware can be much cheaper than software in most cases because software requires more advanced hardware to be usable at all. You can blink an LED with a Raspberry Pi with software very easily yes, for about $30, but I can blink an LED with $0.30 worth of analog components just as easily. Sometimes you just need the simplest and cheapest solution and that won't always involve using hardware that can support running software. It goes this way more than you think it does.

EDIT: More...

Also, adding a few extra components to a design costs way less than setting up an additional manufacturing step that involves loading the firmware and testing it out. Software isn't free because you now need to employ software engineers. If you have a pure hardware design then you already have the electronic engineers on staff. Also, analog audio processing sounds better than digital ever will due to the nature of sound being analog. Digital audio is an approximation of the sound and will always suffer from digital artifacts when the input signal exceeds the parameters of the digital system such as sampling frequency or conversion resolution. And let's not even get into the compression issues....

The audio in "loud" commercials rarely exceeds the FCC allowed limit for volume. The reason they sound loud compared to the normal audio program of the shows they accompany is due to an audio engineering technique called "compression/expansion". A compander which handles both the compression and expansion of the sound has the effect of reducing the overall dynamic range of the audio by amplifying the soft sounds and limiting the loud sounds so all the audio has a more equal loudness at all frequencies. This causes the human brain to interpret the sound as louder than it really is because there is little or no difference between soft and loud sounds. The peak decibel output stays below the FCC limit but the sound is more aggressive. This is used in nearly all music recording now and makes everything sound like shit.
